front: What are the four phases of the business cycle?
back: Expansion (rising GDP and employment), peak (high point, strained capacity, rising inflation), contraction/recession (falling GDP, rising unemployment) and trough (low point before recovery). Cycles recur but are not periodic.

front: How is a recession commonly defined?
back: As a rule of thumb, two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP. Official dating bodies use a broader judgement of a significant, widespread decline in activity lasting more than a few months.
Firms cut production when the inventory-to-sales ratio is too high, deepening a slowdown, then raise production faster than sales to restock when the ratio is too low, helping launch a recovery.

front: Unemployment rate and labour force participation rate formulas
back:
Unemployment rate = unemployed / labour force.
Participation rate = labour force / working-age population.
Labour force = employed + unemployed.

front: Why can the unemployment rate fall without any job creation?
back: Discouraged workers who stop searching leave the labour force, so they are no longer counted as unemployed. The participation rate falls at the same time.

Frictional (normal job search), structural (skills or location mismatch), cyclical (weak aggregate demand) and seasonal. The natural rate has frictional and structural unemployment but no cyclical unemployment.
Disinflation: inflation positive but falling. Deflation: price level falling (negative inflation). Hyperinflation: extremely rapid, accelerating inflation that destroys the value of money.

front: CPI formula and its three measurement biases
back: CPI = (cost of fixed basket at current prices / cost at base prices) x 100. Biases that overstate inflation: substitution bias, new-product bias and quality bias.
Headline inflation includes all items in the index. Core inflation excludes volatile food and energy prices to show the underlying trend.
Demand-pull: aggregate demand exceeds capacity, so too much spending chases too few goods. Cost-push: higher input costs (wages, energy) are passed on to prices; supply shocks can cause stagflation.

front: Leading, coincident and lagging indicators: examples
back: Leading: stock prices, new orders, building permits, yield-curve slope. Coincident: employment, industrial production, personal income. Lagging: duration of unemployment, inventory-to-sales ratio, unit labour costs, prime rate.
